prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map separates the near foreground—main standing person and counter/display surfaces, roughly 0.5–1.2 m away—from the darker walls and corridor, roughly 2–5 m away; these metric ranges are approximate because monocular depth has no visible scale calibration. In frame 1 the standing person is directly ahead and slightly right, within the camera wearer’s arm reach or just beyond it, while the snack rack is left and about 0.8–1.5 m away; in frames 2–3 the view turns right toward a display case about 0.5–1.2 m away, with a partly occluded seated person approximately 1.5–3 m beyond it. Frames 4–5 return to the standing person at about the same close distance, facing generally toward the camera with the head angled downward rather than clear eye contact; another person is partly cut off at the far right of frame 5, likely about 1–2 m away and separated from the standing person by roughly 1–2 m laterally. The depth map makes foreground/background ordering and the display case’s occlusion of the seated person clearer than RGB alone, but it is unreliable around silhouettes, reflective glass, cropped edges, and uniformly bright people, and it cannot robustly distinguish sub-metre distances or gaze direction.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks clearly isolate the main person in frames 1, 4, and 5, placing him directly ahead or slightly right at roughly 0.5–1.2 m, with his head above the counter line and torso blocking the background; his frontal silhouette supports that he faces generally toward the camera, although gaze is not recoverable. In frame 2, a large central mask labelled “tv” corresponds spatially to the glass display case, while person fragments appear at its left and right edges, showing that people are partly outside the frame or occluded by the case; the case is within roughly 0.5–1.2 m and the obscured person is farther away, around 1.5–3 m. By frame 3 the case dominates the left foreground and most people are absent or hidden, whereas frames 4–5 bring the main person back close and reveal another partially cropped person at far right, about 1–2 m from the camera and roughly 1–2 m to the main person’s right. Segmentation reveals object extents and occlusion boundaries that are harder to parse in RGB, but labels such as “tv,” “cell phone,” and the cropped “laptop” appear unreliable, several people are split into fragments, and the map provides no direct metric depth or dependable facing direction.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects the main person’s face and upper-body line in frames 1, 4, and 5, confirming that he is close, centered to center-right, upright, and broadly facing the camera; the face keypoints do not establish whether his eyes look directly at the wearer. Frame 1 includes a bent arm descending on the image-left side and another arm extending across the torso, suggesting the hands are near counter height and potentially within about 0.5–1 m of the camera wearer, while frames 4–5 retain only a shoulder/upper-body line and facial landmarks. Frame 2 contains only a small hand skeleton near the lower middle-right, close to the display-case edge, while frame 3 has no pose detection, consistent with bodies being cropped, hidden behind the case, or out of view as the camera turns away and then back. Pose makes limb arrangement, body orientation, and the isolated near hand clearer than RGB alone, but missing joints, absent magenta hand detections, sparse shoulder lines, and failure on occluded people make reach, inter-person distance, and motion direction uncertain.
